title: How Old CRT TVs Painted Pictures With a Beam of Electrons
description: No pixels, no chips — just a single steered beam of electrons redrawing the whole screen thirty times a second. Original AI-narrated commentary exploring how CRT TVs actually worked.

hook_candidates.text: How did an old TV show a moving color picture with zero computer chips inside it?
Every picture on an old CRT TV was already gone before you saw it — redrawn from scratch thirty times a second by a single moving dot.
You think old TVs had pixels like your phone? They didn't — they had one beam of electrons doing all the work.

beats.text: No frame was ever stored. One electron beam swept side to side, redrawing the whole picture from scratch thirty times a second.
beats.broll_query: CRT tube electron gun diagram animation

beats.text: Magnets around the tube neck steered that beam, aiming it at one exact point on the glass at a time.
beats.broll_query: magnetic deflection coils CRT tube macro

beats.text: Hit the phosphor coating and it glowed red, green, or blue for a split second, so the beam kept racing back to refresh it.
beats.broll_query: phosphor screen glowing red green blue macro

beats.text: Your eyes just blended those fast flashes into one smooth, full-color picture.
